speaker: Sean Carroll
title: Sean Carroll: General Relativity, Quantum Mechanics, Black Holes & Aliens (#428)
question: In astrophysics, why are we nowhere close to directly observing Hawking radiation from black holes?
guest: Right now, we are nowhere close to observing Hawking radiation. Here's the sad fact: the larger the black hole is, the lower its temperature is. So a small black hole, like a microscopically small black hole, might be very visible—it's giving off light. But something like the black hole at the center of our galaxy, three million times the mass of the sun, Sagittarius A*, is so cold and low temperature that its radiation will never be observable. Black holes are hard to make. We don't have any nearby. The ones we have out there in the universe are very faint, so there's no immediate hope for detecting Hawking radiation.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because the radiation is fantastically faint for any black hole we know exists. A black hole's Hawking temperature is inversely proportional to its mass: a solar-mass black hole radiates at about 60 billionths of a kelvin, and supermassive ones are colder still by factors of millions to billions. The cosmic microwave background, at 2.7 K, is tens of millions of times hotter, so real astrophysical black holes absorb far more energy than they emit and their thermal glow is hopelessly swamped. Hot accretion disks and surrounding gas add still more contamination.

The emitted power is also absurdly small, roughly 10⁻²⁸ watts for a solar-mass black hole, mostly in photons with wavelengths comparable to the horizon size (kilometres). Detecting that from a source light-years away is far beyond any conceivable instrument.

Only very small black holes would be hot and bright: primordial ones of around 10¹¹–10¹² kg would now be ending their evaporation in bursts of gamma rays. Gamma-ray telescopes have searched for such bursts and found none, so the only evidence so far comes from laboratory analogue systems, not real black holes.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Direct observation of Hawking radiation is far beyond reach because a black hole’s temperature and luminosity scale inversely with its mass, making every known astrophysical black hole extraordinarily cold and dim. A stellar-mass black hole has a temperature of mere tens of nanokelvins—roughly a hundred million times colder than the 2.7-kelvin cosmic microwave background—while supermassive black holes are millions to billions of times colder still. Consequently, known black holes absorb far more ambient energy than they emit. A typical stellar-mass black hole radiates only about $10^{-29}$ watts in ultra-long radio waves, a whisper completely drowned out by cosmic background radiation, interstellar plasma, and bright emissions from surrounding gas or accretion disks. With the nearest known black holes over 1,500 light-years away, that already minuscule flux is diluted to complete undetectability at Earth. Only hypothetical, low-mass primordial black holes formed in the early universe would be small and hot enough to emit observable X-rays or gamma rays, and none have ever been found.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The basic problem is that Hawking radiation from any black hole we know of is extremely faint and extremely cold. The temperature goes down as the mass goes up. A black hole with the Sun's mass has a Hawking temperature of about 60 billionths of a kelvin, and real stellar black holes, at roughly 5 to 100 solar masses, are colder still. Supermassive black holes are colder by many more orders of magnitude.

The cosmic microwave background is about 2.7 K, so every known black hole takes in far more energy from its surroundings than it gives off. A solar-mass black hole would radiate only about 10⁻²⁸ watts in total, mostly as radio waves with wavelengths around the size of the black hole. That signal would also be buried under the bright X-rays from hot gas falling into the black hole.

The one realistic hope is small primordial black holes from the early universe, if they exist. One of about 10¹¹–10¹² kg would be finishing its evaporation now in a final burst of gamma rays. Instruments such as Fermi and HAWC have looked for those bursts and found none. Lab "analog black holes," such as sound horizons in Bose–Einstein condensates, have produced Hawking-like signals, but that is only indirect support.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Astrophysical black holes are far too massive to produce detectable Hawking radiation. A black hole’s Hawking temperature is inversely proportional to its mass: a solar-mass black hole has a temperature of only about 60 nanokelvin, and supermassive black holes are millions to billions of times colder still. The total emitted power is correspondingly minuscule—roughly 10⁻²⁸ watts for a solar-mass black hole—and arrives across astronomical distances as vanishingly faint, ultra-long-wavelength photons.

Even more decisively, this signal is completely buried in background noise. The cosmic microwave background fills all of space at about 2.7 kelvin, tens of millions of times hotter than any known black hole, so astrophysical black holes absorb vastly more radiation than they emit. Accretion disks, starlight, and interstellar plasma add further orders of magnitude of interference. Only much smaller, hypothetical primordial black holes—roughly asteroid-mass or lighter—would be hot and bright enough to observe directly, and none have been confirmed to exist.
